Chained Price Index

Source: R/priceIndex.R
chainedIndex.Rd

Price index over several periods for a panel of items in long format. For every pair of adjacent periods a bilateral index is computed on the items observed in both periods (matched items), and these links are multiplied up to the chained index. Items may thus enter and leave the basket over time, and the weights are updated with every link.

Usage

chainedIndex(
  p,
  id,
  period,
  q = NULL,
  estimator = c("laspeyres", "paasche", "fisher", "tornqvist", "walsh",
    "marshall-edgeworth", "drobisch", "sato-vartia", "geo-laspeyres", "geo-paasche",
    "palgrave", "jevons", "carli", "dutot"),
  base = NULL,
  na.rm = FALSE
)

Arguments

p

numeric vector of prices, one value per item and period

id

vector identifying the item of each price

period

vector identifying the period of each price, of any sortable type (numeric, Date, factor, ...)

q

numeric vector of quantities belonging to p, or NULL for the unweighted estimators

estimator

the index formula used for the links, see priceIndex()

base

the period in which the index is set to 1. Defaults to the first period.

na.rm

logical, should records with a missing price or quantity be removed? Defaults to FALSE, in which case a link involving a missing value is NA.

Value

A data frame with one row per period and the columns

period

the period

index

the chained index, 1 in the base period

link

the bilateral index against the previous period, NA in the first period

n

the number of matched items the link is based on

Details

The periods are taken in the sort order of period (level order for a factor). A link between two periods without any common item is not defined; it is returned as NA with a warning, and so is the index beyond that break as seen from the base period.

New and disappearing items do not contribute to the link in which they enter or leave. Whether an item is the same over time is decided by id alone, so the choice of the item level matters: at the level of the single package a switch from an original to a cheaper generic is a change of the basket, at the level of the substance (with unit values as prices) it is a price decrease.

References

Balk, B. M. (2008). Price and Quantity Index Numbers: Models for Measuring Aggregate Change and Difference. Cambridge University Press.

Diewert, W. E. (1976). Exact and superlative index numbers. Journal of Econometrics, 4(2), 115–145.

ILO, IMF, OECD, UNECE, Eurostat and World Bank (2004). Consumer Price Index Manual: Theory and Practice. International Labour Office, Geneva.

See also

priceIndex() for the bilateral indices and their formulas

Other index.price: priceIndex()

Examples

# item "d" enters in 2021, item "c" leaves after 2021
d <- data.frame(
  year = c(2020, 2020, 2020, 2021, 2021, 2021, 2021, 2022, 2022, 2022),
  id   = c("a", "b", "c", "a", "b", "c", "d", "a", "b", "d"),
  p    = c(2.0, 5.0, 10.0, 2.2, 5.5, 9.0, 20.0, 2.1, 5.6, 16.0),
  q    = c(100, 40, 10, 90, 45, 14, 5, 95, 40, 12)
)

chainedIndex(d$p, d$id, d$year, d$q, estimator = "tornqvist")
#>   period    index      link  n
#> 1   2020 1.000000        NA NA
#> 2   2021 1.054558 1.0545582  3
#> 3   2022 0.989307 0.9381246  3
##   period    index      link  n
## 1   2020 1.000000        NA NA
## 2   2021 1.054558 1.0545582  3
## 3   2022 0.989307 0.9381246  3

# unweighted, rebased to 2022
chainedIndex(d$p, d$id, d$year, estimator = "jevons", base = 2022)
#>   period    index     link  n
#> 1   2020 1.057029       NA NA
#> 2   2021 1.087500 1.028828  3
#> 3   2022 1.000000 0.919540  3
